9bdbea62-8e72-8e60-4813-875637e716b0/en/.text: This is chapter 1 of our postgraduate PINNs session: from physics to a trainable function.
We will connect heat problem to field network.
Finally, we will use physics residual to check what we have learned.
Before defining the mathematics, let us start with the practical question that makes physical constraints useful when measurements are sparse.
Physics-informed neural networks, or PINNs, combine a function model with physical constraints.
Imagine a heated rod with only a few temperature sensors.
The left part of our schematic represents measurements, and the right part represents information supplied by an equation.
We want a continuous temperature field between sensors, rather than an unconstrained collection of guesses.
This is a modelling strategy, not a promise to outperform a numerical solver.
Our route is to formulate one heat problem, turn its equation into a differentiable residual, train a network, and then test both accurate and misleading answers.
Later we will infer an unknown coefficient.
Keep asking what information selects the solution and what evidence would justify trusting it.
We have motivated combining measurements with physics, so we now need a precise evolution law that tells our temperature model what physically consistent behaviour means.
The heat equation is a partial differential equation, or PDE.
Here x is position, t is time, and u of x and t is temperature relative to a reference level.
Our teaching coordinates and temperature are dimensionless.
Alpha is the effective diffusion coefficient, set to zero point one in the forward experiment.
A subscript t means a first time derivative, and x x means a second spatial derivative.
The coloured rod and the curve below it show the same temperature profile evolving from a warm middle with both ends held cold.
Orange means warmer, blue means colder, and the dashed curve preserves the initial sine profile for comparison.
Watch the middle cool as heat flows toward the cold ends, while the solid temperature curve decays without changing its sine shape.
The two schematic quantities explain the equation together: local temperature changes in proportion to spatial curvature.
Positive alpha smooths a profile.
A straight spatial profile has zero curvature and therefore no local change under this equation.
But the evolution law does not specify how the rod starts or how its ends are held.
Those conditions select a particular experiment.
The heat equation tells our model how temperature evolves, but it cannot select the starting profile or endpoint temperatures, which is why we now introduce initial and boundary conditions.
The first expression fixes the initial temperature profile at time zero.
Pi is the circle constant and x remains the position.
The second expression fixes both endpoints at zero for every time, a Dirichlet boundary condition.
In space-time these are distinct sets: one initial line and two boundary lines, represented by the two schematic parts.
Two functions can satisfy the same heat equation while describing different starting profiles.
They solve different experiments even if both have zero interior residual.
We therefore need an equation constraint, an initial constraint and a boundary constraint.
Keep their roles separate, because each will become its own training term.
Next we choose a case with an exact reference solution so our numerical claims can be checked.
We have specified the equation and its conditions, and an exact solution will now give us a way to check whether a trained model actually solves that particular problem.
The star marks a reference solution, not a learned parameter.
The sine factor gives spatial shape and the exponential factor gives temporal decay.
Differentiating in time produces minus alpha pi squared, while two spatial derivatives of the sine produce minus pi squared.
Thus the two sides of the heat equation agree, directly connecting each factor in the schematic to the equation.
At time zero the exponential is one, and the sine vanishes at both endpoints, so the conditions also hold.
During forward training we withhold these interior reference values.
Afterwards they provide an independent test of solution error.
That separation matters: minimising the training objective and recovering the correct physical field are related but different achievements.
The exact solution shows how diffusivity controls temperature, which lets us distinguish predicting a field from a known coefficient and inferring an unknown coefficient from measurements.
In a forward problem alpha and the conditions are known, and the temperature field is unknown.
In an inverse problem, u subscript obs denotes observed temperatures, and alpha becomes an additional unknown.
The arrows describe inference, not a guarantee that any small dataset identifies the coefficient.
The same residual machinery can support both tasks.
For example, observations only at time zero do not identify alpha in our example because the prescribed initial sine does not depend on it.
Positive-time measurements contain decay information, although noise can weaken the inference.
We will solve the forward case first and return to this information question before jointly fitting a field and coefficient.
We now know which quantities each task must recover, so the next step is to choose how a neural network will represent the unknown temperature field.
Theta denotes all trainable weights and biases.
The subscript on u labels a neural prediction rather than the exact solution.
One coordinate pair produces one predicted temperature, and many queries describe a continuous field.
All these predictions share theta, so this is not a separate free value at each training location.
Shared parameters allow a constraint at one location to influence other predictions through an update.
They also make training a coupled optimisation problem.
We use smooth hyperbolic-tangent activations because the residual requires second coordinate derivatives.
Expressive function classes do not guarantee successful optimisation, a distinction we will revisit when the network produces an apparently plausible but incorrect field.
The network gives us a temperature prediction, but we still need a computable test of whether that prediction obeys the heat equation, so we construct the residual.
The letter r denotes a residual: substitute the predicted field into the heat equation and move all terms to one side.
Partial t and partial x x are coordinate derivatives, not updates of theta.
Residual zero means predicted time change agrees with alpha times predicted curvature at that queried location.
The schematic therefore interprets the formula as a test of local consistency.
It does not test whether we chose the correct initial state.
Nor does a small residual averaged over finitely many points prove that it is small everywhere.
We now have the central PINN mechanism, but the next prediction question exposes exactly why residual information must be combined with conditions.
We have defined residual zero as local equation consistency, and a simple zero-field prediction will now test whether that condition is enough to identify our intended experiment.
Before seeing any training curves, suppose the network predicts zero temperature everywhere.
Its derivatives are zero, so its residual is zero.
It also satisfies both endpoint values.
Is it the solution of our experiment?
Use the initial sine profile to decide rather than treating residual zero as a sufficient certificate.
Work in pairs for two minutes: list the requirements it satisfies and the one it violates.
The answer is that the interior initial temperatures are wrong, so this is not our solution.
We will later train an intentionally incomplete model to see this failure numerically.
Next we implement the derivatives and the separate loss terms that prevent it.

66ca6674-77b3-0ea0-f19e-74d8b4e71e2e/en/.text: This is chapter 2 of our postgraduate PINNs session: from derivatives to the training objective.
We will connect derivatives to conditions.
Finally, we will use objective to check what we have learned.
The zero-field example showed why we need more than an equation residual, and before assembling all the losses we must choose a network whose coordinate derivatives can actually be computed.
Here q is the column vector of coordinates, h is a hidden-layer output, W is a weight matrix, and b is a bias vector.
The superscript T denotes transpose, turning the written coordinate pair into a column.
The schematic follows the same mapping as the equation: a linear combination of coordinates is passed through the smooth hyperbolic tangent.
We need this smoothness because the heat residual contains a second spatial derivative.
A standard ReLU network is piecewise linear in its inputs, so its second derivative is zero almost everywhere and problematic at the kinks for this strong-form residual.
That does not prohibit every piecewise-linear scientific model, but it motivates a smooth choice here.
Next we see how a computational graph supplies derivatives without finite differences.
A smooth network makes the required derivatives meaningful, and automatic differentiation now supplies a practical way to evaluate them through the computation graph.
The symbols d u over d h and d h over d x describe sensitivities along two edges of a computation.
Here we temporarily consider a scalar chain to make the rule visible.

Automatic differentiation applies this chain rule to recorded elementary operations, evaluating derivatives of the represented numerical function rather than perturbing the coordinate by a small step.
It is not symbolic algebra that necessarily produces a human-readable expression, and it is not immune to floating-point error.
It also differentiates the network we actually built, not the true physical field.
In a PINN we apply the mechanism once for first coordinate derivatives and again for second derivatives.
Keeping the graph of the first derivative is therefore essential.
We have seen how the chain rule computes derivatives, but we must separate derivatives with respect to coordinates from gradients that update the network parameters.
Partial x u theta tells us how the current predicted field changes as position changes while theta is held fixed.
Nabla theta L is the gradient of the training loss with respect to all trainable weights and biases.
L denotes the objective we will construct shortly.
The two schematic roles prevent a common confusion: evaluating a PDE derivative is not itself a learning step.
First the network and coordinate derivatives form the residual and the scalar loss.
Then backpropagation differentiates that loss with respect to theta, and the optimiser updates theta.
Consequently the coordinate-derivative operations must remain differentiable with respect to parameters.
In PyTorch, create graph equals true provides the graph needed to differentiate through these derivatives during training.
With the roles of coordinate and parameter derivatives separated, we can now translate the heat residual into tensor operations without confusing equation evaluation with learning.
In our implementation the input tensor has two columns in the fixed order x then t.
One gradient call returns both u x and u t, and a second call differentiates u x with respect to the coordinates and keeps its x component.
Subtracting alpha times u x x from u t gives the same residual we derived on the previous chapter, now as executable tensor operations.
The convenient gradient of summed outputs gives per-point coordinate derivatives only because our model processes input rows independently.
Layers that couple samples require more careful Jacobian treatment.
We explicitly enable gradients on input coordinates and use ones like u as the vector argument to autograd.
The runnable source accompanies the lecture, so the shorthand on the board can be checked against actual code.
We can compute the differential residual, but the zero-field counterexample still passes that test, so we next penalise disagreement with the prescribed initial profile.
L subscript zero is the initial-condition loss, N subscript zero is the number of initial samples, and i indexes those samples.
At each sampled position x i and time zero we compare the prediction against the prescribed sine.
The squared difference penalises both overprediction and underprediction, and averaging prevents the term from simply scaling with the sample count.
The schematic identifies the two quantities being compared inside the brackets.
These temperatures are allowed training targets because they are part of the problem specification, not withheld interior answers.
A zero field gives zero PDE residual but a positive initial loss.
Thus this term directly rules out the counterexample from the first chapter.
We next impose the endpoint requirements separately.
Initial loss constrains how the experiment starts, while the rod endpoints must also remain correct throughout time, which requires a separate boundary loss.
L subscript b denotes boundary loss and N subscript b counts sampled times.
At every selected time t i we penalise the prediction at both endpoints against their known target zero.
The factor two in the denominator accounts for the two endpoint values per sampled time.
The two nodes show exactly which locations the equation evaluates.
This soft penalty encourages small endpoint error but does not make the constraints exact at every time.
Adding more boundary samples changes the empirical coverage, while changing its weight changes the optimisation trade-off.
Later we will compare this with a hard boundary construction that makes endpoint values zero by design.
First we combine the separate losses without losing track of their physical roles.
The equation, initial state and endpoints now each have a measurable error, so we combine them into one objective while keeping their distinct roles visible.
L r is the average squared PDE residual at interior collocation points, L zero is initial loss and L b is boundary loss.
Lambda r, lambda zero and lambda b are nonnegative weights, not the physical diffusivity alpha.
In the forward lab we use weights one, ten and one respectively.
The schematic groups equation consistency and condition matching while the formula keeps all three contributions explicit.
A scalar total is convenient for optimisation, but it can hide an unsatisfied component.
Always log the terms separately and inspect their physical errors as well as their numerical values.
Their units and gradient magnitudes may differ, so equal weights need not mean equal influence.
We will revisit scaling and gradient imbalance after a first working implementation.
We have assembled the full objective, and deliberately removing one term will test whether we understand which information each contribution supplies.
Here the label incomplete means we intentionally omitted initial loss.
Work for three minutes: give a function that makes both retained terms zero but is not the required solution, then write the corrected objective.
State whether increasing interior collocation points alone would remove your counterexample.
Explain using the physics, not just the algebra of the loss.
The zero field is again a counterexample, and more interior points do not help because it satisfies the PDE everywhere.
Restoring the initial requirement changes the problem rather than merely improving sampling.
For an additional check, describe how a wrong nonzero initial amplitude could also solve a different heat experiment.
The next chapter turns this objective into a reproducible training and validation procedure.

f28a2cdd-b9cc-4195-579f-9376a27e3c1b/en/.text: This is chapter 3 of our postgraduate PINNs session: train, validate and test the forward problem.
We will connect scaling to training.
Finally, we will use validation to check what we have learned.
We know which losses are needed, but their numerical behaviour depends on coordinate scales, so we first check the units before running an optimiser.
The hats denote dimensionless variables.
Here x physical and t physical are measured position and time, L is a characteristic length, and T is a characteristic time.
Dividing by these scales brings coordinate ranges to useful numerical magnitudes.
Our earlier unit-domain example had already undergone this step, which is why its coordinates had no physical units.
Do not simply normalise inputs and keep an unchanged physical differential equation.
Coordinate derivatives acquire chain-rule factors, so preprocessing must be reflected in the residual.
Temperature can similarly be scaled by a characteristic difference, using a reference offset when appropriate.
This is a physical consistency requirement before it is an optimisation convenience, and the next equation makes the coefficient change explicit.
Rescaling coordinates also rescales their derivatives, so we must now derive the transformed diffusion coefficient rather than silently training with the old equation.
Alpha physical has dimensions of length squared per time, while alpha hat is dimensionless.
A time derivative contributes one over T and two spatial derivatives contribute one over L squared.
Cancelling the temperature scale yields the coefficient alpha physical times T divided by L squared.
The schematic is a dimensional explanation of the same equation, not an extra empirical correction.
Choosing T equal to L squared divided by alpha physical makes this coefficient one when alpha is known.
In an inverse problem that choice can depend on the very unknown we seek, so use fixed documented reference scales instead.
Scaling can improve conditioning but does not solve every training pathology.
After checking the algebra and units, we can choose the actual sample locations.
With the scaled equation consistent, we next choose where to evaluate its residual and separate those locations from points carrying known temperature values.
N subscript r is the number of interior residual samples and i indexes them.
At each coordinate pair we evaluate the differential equation using the current network;
we do not supply the true interior temperature.
Initial and boundary samples are separate because they enforce separate information.
In our lab the interior sample set is held fixed to make comparisons reproducible.
Random resampling and residual-guided sampling are alternative design choices.
Neither justifies checking only training locations.
A finite collection of small residuals can miss difficult regions, so independent probes must use different points.
Before adding a sophisticated sampling strategy, confirm that each sample set covers the intended part of the domain and that no evaluation labels leak into optimisation.
The sample locations define what the objective checks, and we can now put prediction, differentiation, loss evaluation and parameter updates into one training loop.
Eta is a learning-rate scale, and the left arrow means replacing the parameter vector by an updated value.
The displayed rule is a simple gradient-descent illustration;
our executable run uses Adam, which also maintains moment estimates.
A training step queries the network, forms coordinate derivatives and losses, clears old parameter gradients, backpropagates the loss, and updates the parameters.
Clearing gradients matters because PyTorch normally accumulates them.
Logging detached numerical values avoids accidentally storing an entire history of computation graphs.
Reproducibility also requires a seed, architecture, dtype, sample counts and optimiser settings.
Our logs record these alongside held-out errors, so a smooth-looking animation cannot substitute for a verifiable numerical experiment.
The loop tells us when parameters are updated, but the update method itself is a separate choice, so we compare the roles of Adam and quasi-Newton refinement.
Adam is an adaptive first-order optimiser.
L-BFGS is a limited-memory quasi-Newton method that uses curvature information estimated from optimisation history.
Many PINN workflows use an Adam phase and sometimes an L-BFGS refinement, but this is a practical option rather than a universal rule.
Our logged teaching runs deliberately use Adam alone so the implementation remains short and reproducible.
If trying L-BFGS, inspect its closure requirements, line-search behaviour and compatibility with changing samples.
Compare wall-clock time and physical accuracy, not merely iteration counts.
No optimiser fixes a missing condition or an incorrect residual.
That is why we checked the problem formulation first and will evaluate independent errors after training.
An optimiser can only reduce a soft penalty, so we next ask whether the network representation itself can guarantee the endpoint conditions exactly.
V theta is an unconstrained smooth neural function.
Multiplying it by x times one minus x makes the temperature exactly zero at x equal to zero and one, regardless of its parameters.
This hard construction enforces our homogeneous endpoint values by algebra rather than a finite penalty.
The diagram shows why the factor, not optimiser success, gives the guarantee.
It does not automatically enforce the initial sine profile, and it changes the derivatives entering the residual.
Always differentiate the full constructed u rather than only v.
Hard constraints can be useful when a suitable construction is available, but complicated geometries and boundary types may require more care.
Our main run keeps soft conditions to make their separate training errors visible.
Even exact endpoints would not guarantee an accurate interior field, so we now define independent checks that can distinguish a low training loss from a correct solution.
E subscript rel is relative error, and the norm here is the Euclidean norm of values on a held-out space-time grid.
The reference u star is available only because we chose a solvable teaching example.
The evaluation grid is different from all training points.
We also probe residuals on a separate random set and inspect initial and boundary behaviour.
This is a discrete relative L two estimate, not an exact continuous norm.
If no analytical reference exists, use trusted numerical convergence studies, conservation checks, held-out observations and sensitivity tests instead.
A single low training loss is insufficient.
We now have enough safeguards to look at an actual training trace without mistaking a visual fit for evidence.
We now have a training procedure and independent evaluation criteria, so we can interpret an actual Python training trace rather than judging success from a curve alone.
The code panel describes the actual local PyTorch run, and the graph replays saved training checkpoints rather than simulating improvement.
Epoch means one parameter-update iteration in this full-batch teaching run.
The blue reference curve is the exact temperature at time one half, and the yellow curve is the network prediction at that same time.
The displayed relative error uses the full held-out space-time grid, not just the curve.
As the professor speaks, checkpoints advance and the logged losses and error change.
Read the initial loss separately from the residual and boundary loss.
A visually close time slice is encouraging but not a complete test, because errors elsewhere could remain.
After the narrated replay, use the downloadable code to reproduce the seed and compare its final metrics.
The following activity asks you to design a more convincing validation.
The replay showed one successful run, but one time slice is limited evidence, so your next task is to design checks that could expose errors elsewhere.
Allow four minutes to design three independent checks for this forward problem.
At least one must examine conditions, one must examine the interior, and one must avoid using the training point set.
Say which check is possible only because the example has an analytical solution.
If the temperature curve looks correct at time one half, explain why that alone does not validate all times.

A strong answer includes held-out relative error across space-time, independently sampled residuals, and explicit initial or boundary checks, with multiple seeds or sampling sensitivities as an additional investigation.
These checks answer different questions and should not be collapsed into a single number.
After a ten-minute break, we will reuse the same machinery to infer alpha rather than treating it as known.

edc4ab3c-c2b0-bfb2-d735-b535bff25688/en/.text: This is chapter 4 of our postgraduate PINNs session: infer a physical parameter from observations.
We will connect coefficient to observations.
Finally, we will use sensitivity to check what we have learned.
The forward workflow recovered a field with known diffusivity, and we now ask what extra information is needed when diffusivity itself must be learned.
The residual now carries two unknowns: the network parameters theta and the physical coefficient alpha.
Alpha remains one positive scalar in this example, not a separate value at every point.
The same temperature derivatives that constrain the field also constrain the coefficient.
But the equation alone can admit many field-and-coefficient pairs, so we need observations that contain information about diffusion.
We retain the known initial and boundary conditions and add temperatures at selected positive times.
Treat this as joint model calibration, not a magical conversion of any dataset into a physical constant.
The question is whether distinct alpha values can be distinguished after accounting for field flexibility and measurement noise.
We first write exactly how these observations enter the objective.
The equation alone does not select a unique field and coefficient pair, so we next specify how measured temperatures constrain that joint inverse problem.
L subscript d is data loss, N d is the number of observations, and y i is the measured temperature at coordinate pair x i, t i.
The prediction must be queried at exactly those coordinates.
In the synthetic inverse run, sixty-four interior observations are generated from the exact solution with additive Gaussian noise of standard deviation zero point zero zero five.
The true coefficient is known to us because we created the experiment, but it is not supplied as a training target.
Observations are different from residual-only collocation points, and withheld reference values are still reserved for evaluation.
Confusing these roles makes an inverse result look more convincing than it is.
We next enforce the prior physical requirement that diffusivity be positive.
Measurements provide information about the coefficient, but our parameterisation must also respect positive diffusivity, so we introduce a positive transformation before fitting it.
Beta is a freely optimised real scalar and epsilon is a small fixed positive offset, one millionth in our code.
The logarithmic expression is the softplus function, evaluated with a numerically stable library routine.
This transformation makes alpha positive for every beta and avoids clipping a parameter after each update.
The diagram maps a mathematical optimisation variable to a physically admissible coefficient.
Positivity is a modelling assumption appropriate for this diffusion problem, not evidence that the inferred magnitude is correct.
It also changes parameter sensitivities through the chain rule, and extreme beta values can have small gradients.
Record the transformation and initialisation when reporting the experiment.
We then optimise this scalar and the network parameters together while keeping their meanings distinct.
We can now represent a positive coefficient and compare predictions with observations, which lets us combine both unknowns in one differentiable fitting objective.
The minimum is over theta and beta, with alpha obtained through the positive transformation.
The displayed weights are our teaching-run settings, not universal defaults.
Data loss ties the field to observed temperatures, conditions select the physical experiment, and the residual links the field derivatives to alpha.
Both kinds of parameter receive gradients through that combined computation.
There can be compensation between a distorted field and a distorted coefficient.
A small joint objective does not establish uniqueness or calibrated uncertainty.
Evaluate field error and coefficient error separately when a synthetic truth is available, then repeat across noise realisations and initialisations for a stronger investigation.
Before interpreting a fitted number, ask which observation times could have distinguished it.
A joint objective tells us how to fit a coefficient, but not whether measurements can distinguish it, so we now examine parameter sensitivity.
The partial derivative with respect to alpha measures how much the predicted reference temperature changes when diffusivity changes.
Differentiating our exact sine-mode solution gives minus pi squared times t times u star.
At time zero this sensitivity vanishes.
At rod endpoints the temperature also vanishes, so those homogeneous endpoint readings provide no diffusivity information in this example.
At positive interior locations there is information, but later is not always better: if the temperature has decayed near the noise floor, measurements become weak again.
This is an example-specific sensitivity calculation, not a general theorem about every inverse PDE.
It tells us to choose observation times and locations using the forward physics rather than selecting sensors only for convenience.
Sensitivity identified informative measurement locations, but noisy readings can still produce an unstable estimate, so we must separate a fitted number from trustworthy uncertainty.
Epsilon i denotes observation noise, distinct from the small positivity offset used earlier.
In our synthetic dataset this noise is independent zero-mean Gaussian with known chosen scale.
A fitted alpha is a point estimate conditioned on that dataset, architecture, objective and optimiser.
Reporting extra decimal places does not make it more reliable.
To assess stability, regenerate noise, resample sensors and restart training with different seeds.
More formal uncertainty methods require additional modelling assumptions and validation.
We do not claim calibrated confidence intervals from this one demonstration.
Its purpose is to show a reproducible joint inverse fit and to make the difference between known synthetic truth and uncertain real-world inference explicit.
With the objective, information requirements and noise limitations clear, we can now interpret the actual joint-training trace for the field and diffusivity.
The code and animation now use the inverse run rather than the forward run.
The displayed alpha is transformed from the learned beta at each saved checkpoint, and its reference value zero point one is used only for evaluation.
Temperature curves still correspond to time one half.
Watch both the coefficient and the held-out field error, because improvement in one does not logically guarantee improvement in the other.
This particular seeded run recovers a coefficient close to the synthetic value.
That is evidence about a small controlled example, not proof of general identifiability.
Reproduce the run, then remove positive-time observations or increase noise to test its dependence on information.
The following exercise asks you to predict those outcomes before changing the code.
The inverse replay recovered one synthetic coefficient, and the next exercise tests whether you can predict which sensor choices would remove the information that made recovery possible.
Allow three minutes to choose between three datasets: initial-time temperatures only, endpoint temperatures only, or interior temperatures at several positive times.
Explain your choice using the sensitivity formula, and identify a time range that could become uninformative after strong decay.
Then say what you would report if several alpha values fit equally well.
The third dataset can contain useful coefficient information, while the first two do not for this exact setup.
If distinct coefficients remain consistent with observations, report the ambiguity rather than a falsely precise estimate.
We now have a working forward and inverse workflow.
The next chapter examines why the same formal ingredients can still produce serious optimisation and approximation failures.

479020db-859a-8b53-6ed9-b3afc6ee9374/en/.text: This is chapter 5 of our postgraduate PINNs session: failure modes, diagnosis and remedies.
We will connect failure to pathologies.
Finally, we will use diagnosis to check what we have learned.
The forward and inverse examples worked under controlled settings, but we now need to understand why a small residual can coexist with a seriously wrong solution.
The crossed implication means the statement on the left is not sufficient to establish the statement on the right.
A residual checks a differential relation, whereas solution error compares with the specific field selected by all conditions.
Our zero-field counterexample makes this distinction without any optimisation theory: the PDE and endpoints can be satisfied while the initial profile is wrong.
Even with all losses present, finite sampling, unstable formulations and unsuccessful optimisation can obstruct accuracy.
Error bounds require assumptions about the problem, stability and residual norms, rather than an unqualified statement that small loss implies correctness.
Diagnose what information and numerical evidence are actually available before attributing every failure to network size.
Missing information is one cause of error, but even a complete objective can train unevenly, so we next inspect how its component gradients compete.
Here j indexes loss components and g j is the norm of the weighted component gradient with respect to network parameters.
The lambda weights are numerical trade-offs, not physical coefficients.
Two losses with similar scalar values can produce very different gradients, and their gradient directions can oppose one another.
That is why looking only at the total curve can miss a neglected physical requirement.
As a diagnosis, record individual values, physical constraint errors and representative gradient magnitudes or directions.
Reweighting, rescaling or curriculum changes may help particular problems, but they should be evaluated by independent solution metrics.
A weighting method that merely makes curves look similar is not enough.
This is a training interaction, separate from whether the function class can express the solution.
Gradient imbalance concerns the interaction between objectives, while spatial frequency changes derivative scales themselves, so we next examine that separate source of difficulty.
K is a positive integer frequency index.
A higher k produces more spatial oscillations, and the second derivative multiplies their amplitude by k pi squared.
Squaring a residual can therefore create strong frequency-dependent numerical scales.
The schematic connects oscillatory structure to derivative amplification, showing one reason a visually small field error may have a large differential effect.
Neural training can also learn some frequency components more slowly than others, often discussed as spectral bias.
Fourier features and different architectures can help selected problems, but the appropriate frequency scales and sampling still matter.
Distinguish the algebraic derivative factor shown here from empirical claims about a particular network or a limiting kernel analysis.
Both motivate tests beyond smooth low-frequency examples.
Spatial structure can create difficult scales, and time-dependent problems add another issue because later predictions depend on an accurate earlier state.
T one and T two mark intermediate time boundaries, while capital T is the final time horizon.
Time-dependent physics propagates information from an initial state.
A global space-time objective may nevertheless reduce later-time residuals before the earlier solution is accurate.
The diagram suggests one alternative: establish an early window and use its endpoint information to support the next.
Sequential windows, causal weighting and curriculum strategies are related ideas, not interchangeable universal cures.
Errors can also propagate across window interfaces, so interface continuity and accumulated error must be checked.
Our short heat experiment does not demonstrate a difficult chaotic regime;
this slide explains a research direction and why longer-time benchmarks require more than reusing the easy training settings.
Time windows change how we organise the temporal problem, and adaptive sampling offers a different intervention by changing where we spend residual-evaluation effort.
The absolute residual can suggest where the current approximation poorly satisfies the equation.
The subscript new denotes proposed additional sample coordinates, not a new physical variable.
A residual-guided strategy allocates computation toward difficult locations rather than adding the same number of points everywhere.
It must still preserve adequate coverage of the domain and conditions.
Changing the sampling distribution can change the effective empirical objective unless weighting is adjusted appropriately.
It can also miss regions where an incorrect field has a deceptively small residual.
Continue reporting independent checks on a fixed evaluation grid or a documented evaluation distribution.
Treat adaptive sampling as a testable intervention rather than proof that all important physics has been found.
We have discussed several possible failure mechanisms, so we now isolate one known cause in a real training run instead of attributing failure to every mechanism at once.
This replay uses a separately executed model trained without initial loss.
The known coefficient and boundary requirement are unchanged, so the experiment isolates an intentionally incomplete objective rather than changing every setting at once.
The blue curve remains the required exact solution, and the yellow curve shows the fitted field.
Inspect the initial error even though it was not included in the optimiser objective.
In this run the network approaches an almost-zero field, with a solution error close to one hundred percent despite a small equation residual.
This is the counterexample we predicted before seeing the code.
It does not establish that every small-loss failure has this cause.
It demonstrates why diagnosing the specified constraints comes before architecture tuning or impressive-looking convergence plots.
The omitted-condition run gave us a known failure cause, and we now need an investigation procedure for cases where the cause is not known in advance.

A useful diagnosis order is to check the physical problem and conditions, verify derivative code on a known function, inspect scaling and loss components, and finally examine independent field errors.
The arrows show an investigation order, not a causal theorem.
A model that violates boundary data needs a different investigation from one with accurate boundaries but oscillatory interior error.
For three minutes, choose a symptom and propose one controlled change plus a metric that could falsify your explanation.
Examples include restoring a missing initial term, checking a coordinate-column swap, or comparing held-out residuals after changing sampling.
State what outcome would make you reject your diagnosis.
This habit leads naturally to the research experiment design in the final chapter.
A diagnosis proposes a cause, but a remedy is convincing only if a controlled comparison can test that proposal, so we now define the baseline and intervention.
Delta E is the change in a documented evaluation error between a baseline and an intervention.
An apparent improvement should be interpreted alongside repeated seeds, runtime, sampling budget and all changed hyperparameters.
Keeping the differential problem fixed matters: solving an easier equation is not a fair demonstration that an optimiser has improved on the original problem.
An ablation removes or changes one component to test its contribution, while a sensitivity study varies a setting systematically.
Neither is supplied by one successful screenshot.
We have shown one intentionally controlled failure and a compact forward and inverse run.
The final chapter broadens the PDE and research context without claiming these tiny experiments establish performance on harder applications.

We will connect new equations to comparisons.
